Red Hat Enterprise Linux System Administration I | Study file

This chapter teaches you to see what is running on a Linux system and to control it. You learn how to list processes, manage several jobs in one terminal, stop processes with signals, and read the system load.
Topics in this chapter, in book order:

8.2 How a process is created: fork, exec and zombies
A new process is made by copying a parent (fork), and the copy then runs its own program (exec).
Think of a photocopier. You photocopy a worker's whole desk, then give the copy a new task. The copy is the

Every process has a state that tells you what it is doing right now.

A signal is a message sent to a process to make it do something, such as stop or end.
Think of tapping a worker on the shoulder. Some taps say "please finish up". One says "stop now" and cannot be ignored.
is a software interrupt delivered to a process. It can come from an error, an outside event (like a timer ending), or your own request. You can name a signal by its short name (
Each signal has a default action:
(save a memory image called a core dump, then end), or
(suspend and wait). A program can add a
to ignore or change the default.
Keys signal the foreground process: Ctrl+Z suspends, Ctrl+C ends, Ctrl+\ ends with a core dump. For a background process or another session, use a command (8.10).
The table below lists the main signals for routine work.
"Cannot be blocked" means the program cannot refuse or ignore it.
The numbers are for x86_64 systems.
TERM asks politely, KILL forces, STOP and CONT pause and resume.
Reports that a terminal's controlling process ended. Also asks a process to reload its configuration without ending.
Keyboard interrupt (Ctrl+C). Ends the program. Can be blocked or handled.
Keyboard quit (Ctrl+\). Like INT, and also makes a core dump.
Ends the program abruptly. Cannot be blocked, ignored or handled. Always fatal.
The default signal. Asks the program to end. Can be blocked or handled. The polite way, because the program can clean up first.
Continues a stopped process. Cannot be blocked.
Suspends the process. Cannot be blocked or handled.
Keyboard stop (Ctrl+Z). Unlike STOP, it can be blocked, ignored or handled.
Tip: Signal numbers differ between hardware platforms, but the names and meanings are standard. Use signal names, not numbers, in commands.

Find the session, list the processes, then signal them. Start gently.
SIGKILL ends processes at once with no clean-up. Any unsaved work of those processes is lost.
SIGKILL is often used too quickly. It cannot be handled or ignored, but it stops a process from running its clean-up. Send SIGTERM first, then try SIGINT, and use SIGKILL only if both fail.
Load average is a rough number for how many processes are waiting for the CPU or for slow disk or network work.
Think of a checkout line. Customers are processes. A long line means a slow shop.
Every five seconds the kernel counts the processes that are runnable (state R) or in uninterruptible sleep (state D). It reports the result as an
(recent values count more than old ones) over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes.
Linux also counts processes waiting for disk or network, not only the CPU. So if the load is high but CPU activity is low, look at disk and network activity.
An idle CPU has a load of 0. Each process waiting adds 1. One process running alone counts as 1.

The three numbers are the load over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes.
Compare them to see if load is rising or falling. Here the 1-minute value (2.92) is lower than the 15-minute value (5.20), so load is falling.
Load average counts processes waiting for the CPU or for slow I/O.
Divide the load averages by the number of logical CPUs to see whether the system is overloaded.
Think of a shop with four cashiers. A line of four people is fine. A line of eight means waiting. So you compare the line to the number of cashiers.
shows how many CPUs the system has. In the book example it has two cores, two
(two work lanes) per core, so Linux treats it as four CPUs.
A per-CPU value below 1 means good use and little waiting. Above 1 means the resource is full and there is delay.
This simple rule assumes the load comes only from waiting for the CPU. Waiting for disk or network also adds to the load.
